notes:
I've arranged these notes verse by verse, as you asked. My research was cut short by tool limits, so some sections are thin. I didn't reach Guzik's comments on vv. 18–25 at enduringword, the verse-by-verse pages on biblehub, bibleodyssey.org, netbible.org, oca.org, or any Wesleyan, Pentecostal or Lutheran denominational site. I found no notes for vv. 4, 9, 10 or 13–15.

## Verse-by-verse notes

**v. 1**
- **What the opening words mean.** Carson, quoted by Guzik, says the first two words can mean "record of the genealogy," "record of the origins" or "record of the history." Guzik thinks each meaning fits a part of the book: the genealogy (1:1–17), Jesus' origins (1:18–2:23), and the whole Gospel as the history. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-1/
- **Son of David.** Throughout his work, Matthew presents Jesus as the kingly Messiah promised from David's royal line (2 Samuel 7:12-16). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-1/
- **Son of Abraham.** Jesus is the Seed of Abraham in whom all nations would be blessed (Genesis 12:3). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-1/
- **Spurgeon:** the verse shows Matthew's aim. He writes of Jesus AS KING — "the son of David." https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-1-commentary-spurgeon
- **Whose name heads the list.** The HCSB Study Bible note (quoted on Precept Austin) says Old Testament genealogies were named after the earliest ancestor. Naming this one after Jesus, the last descendant, implies he matters more than everyone before him. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-1-commentary
- **Constable** (quoted there) says the same Greek phrase appears in the Greek Old Testament at Genesis 2:4 and 5:1. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-1-commentary

**v. 2**
- **Spurgeon:** the line passed through Isaac rather than Ishmael, and through Jacob rather than Esau the firstborn. He calls readers to observe and admire the sovereignty of God. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-1-commentary-spurgeon

**v. 3 (Tamar)**
- **Guzik:** Tamar posed as a prostitute with her father-in-law Judah and so bore Perez and Zerah (Genesis 38). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-1/
- **A sermon quoted on Precept Austin** says the story is there to show that God uses failures: Through the broken, God breaks through! https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-1-commentary
- **Spurgeon** marvels that the line continued through "this once guilty pair." He sees it as showing how closely the Lord is related to fallen humanity. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-1-commentary-spurgeon

**v. 5 (Rahab, Ruth)**
- **Rahab:** Guzik describes her as a Gentile prostitute whom God went to great lengths to save from judgment and from her way of life. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-1/
- **Ruth:** she came from Moab, a Gentile outside Israel's covenant until she converted. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-1/
- **Why the women are named.** Guzik gives three reasons:
  - Jesus did not come from a pure aristocratic line.
  - He identifies with sinners.
  - Women have a new place under the New Covenant.
  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-1/

**v. 6 (Uriah's wife)**
- **Guzik:** Bathsheba was an adulteress, known for her sin with David. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-1/
- **Carson** (quoted by Guzik) suggests that calling her "Uriah's wife" may point to Uriah being a Hittite, not an Israelite. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-1/

**vv. 7–8**
- **Guzik:** Uzziah was not Joram's son. Three kings come between them (Ahaziah, Joash and Amaziah). He quotes Clarke that such gaps are common in Jewish genealogies. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-1/

**v. 11**
- **Guzik:** Matthew also skips Jehoiakim, who came between Josiah and Jeconiah. Through Jeremiah, God declared that no blood descendant of Jehoiakim would sit on David's throne (Jeremiah 36:30–31). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-1/

**v. 12**
- **Guzik's solution to that curse.** Jesus was Joseph's legal son but not his blood son, so the curse did not touch him. Mary's line came through David's son Nathan, not through Solomon. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/guzik_david/StudyGuide_Mat/Mat_1.cfm

**v. 16**
- **Guzik:** Matthew takes care to show that Joseph was not Jesus' father. He was rather he was the husband of Mary. Guzik quotes R. T. France that the genealogy gives Jesus' legal ancestry, not his physical descent. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/guzik_david/StudyGuide_Mat/Mat_1.cfm
- **Matthew and Luke disagree on Joseph's father.** Two explanations are offered:
  - Jerome answered the emperor Julian's charge of contradiction by saying one Gospel gives Joseph's natural pedigree and the other his legal one.
  - Dr. Barrett proposed that Matthew gives Joseph's line and Luke gives Mary's.
  
  https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-1-commentary

**v. 17**
- **Guzik:** the list is not complete. Matthew edited it into three sets of fourteen so it would be easy to remember. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-1/
- **Spurgeon:** the Holy Spirit chose a rough and simple method to help weak memories. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-1-commentary-spurgeon
- **Zahn's view** (summarised on Precept Austin): the genealogy is a way of summing up history. That would explain the artificial grouping and the naming of brothers and women. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-1-commentary

**v. 18**
- **MacArthur** (quoted by Precept Austin): "birth" comes from the same Greek root as "genealogy" in v. 1. He sees a parallel account of Jesus' origin, this time from his Father's side. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-1-commentary
- **Guzik:** Jewish marriage then had three steps, and Mary was at the betrothal stage. Slanders about Jesus' parentage spread later, including a story about a Roman soldier, and Matthew sets the record straight. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/guzik_david/StudyGuide_Mat/Mat_1.cfm
- **Spurgeon:** He is born of a woman, that he might be human; but not by man, that he might not be sinful. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-1-commentary-spurgeon
- **Precept Austin:** the virgin birth shows that salvation must be God's work, not a human achievement. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-1-commentary

**v. 19**
- **Guzik:** although the couple were not yet formally married, betrothal meant Joseph already counted as Mary's husband. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/guzik_david/StudyGuide_Mat/Mat_1.cfm
- Precept Austin's resources page links to Daniel Wallace, "A Mishnaic Commentary on Matthew 1:19." I didn't read it. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew_1_resources

**v. 20**
- **Guzik:** the dream came while Joseph was still uneasy about his decision. The greeting "son of David" points to Joseph's legal claim to David's throne. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/guzik_david/StudyGuide_Mat/Mat_1.cfm
- **Spurgeon:** the Lord graciously cleared Joseph's suspicion, protecting the mother's honour and the child's welfare. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-1-commentary-spurgeon

**v. 21**
- **Guzik:** Matthew explains the name Jesus in a way that assumes readers know its Hebrew roots. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-1/
- The Berean Annotated Bible glosses the name as "YHWH saves." https://biblehub.com/matthew/1-25.htm

**vv. 22–23**
- **Gill (Baptist):** Jewish translators of the Greek Old Testament rendered Isaiah's word as "virgin" centuries before Matthew. He also reads "Immanuel" as showing that the Messiah is truly God as well as truly man. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/nkj/isaiah/7-14.html
- **Matthew Henry:** "almah" means a virgin in the strict sense, and anything else would not have been the wonderful sign intended. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/1-25.html
- **Barnes:** the name meant God would be with the nation as its protector, and the child's birth would be a sign or pledge of that. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/nkj/isaiah/7-14.html
- **GotQuestions:** "almah" basically means "young woman," and no conclusive argument settles it either way. But the Greek translation's use of "virgin" makes that meaning possible, even likely. It treats Isaiah 7:14 as a double prophecy: first about King Ahaz's situation, then about the Messiah. https://www.gotquestions.org/virgin-or-young-woman.html
- **A Bible Hub Q&A** argues more strongly that every use of "almah" refers to a woman who has not borne children, so "virgin" is not a mistranslation. https://biblehub.com/q/Is_virgin_in_Isaiah_7_14_a_mistranslation.htm

**v. 24**
- **An older commentary on the 1:25 page:** Joseph obeyed the angel promptly, without delay, and willingly, without arguing. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/1-25.htm

**v. 25** (see the debate below)
- **Gill:** Joseph's restraint showed that Mary was a virgin not only when she conceived but also when she gave birth. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/1-25.html
- **Ellicott:** the best manuscripts don't have the word "firstborn." https://biblehub.com/matthew/1-25.htm

## Where Protestant traditions differ

**v. 25: Did Mary remain a virgin after Jesus' birth?**
- **Luther:** catholic.com quotes him saying we should hold that she stayed a virgin, because Scripture doesn't say she lost her virginity. https://www.catholic.com/audio/cot/rebutted-top-objections-to-marys-perpetual-virginity
- **Calvin:** catholic.com articles contradict each other here.
  - One says Calvin held the view.
  - Another says he did not. It quotes him calling a supposed vow of virginity "unfounded and altogether absurd," while also saying the "until" proves nothing about later events.
  
  https://www.catholic.com/magazine/online-edition/apologists-make-mistakes-too
- **Bengel** (Lutheran): "until" doesn't mean relations followed. With regard to the remainder of her married life, the reader is left to form his own opinion. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/1-25.htm
- **Meyer** lists Luther and Calvin among those who held perpetual virginity. He argues this goes against the plain sense of the narrative. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/1-25.htm
- **Clarke** (Methodist): her virginity before Christ's birth is an article of faith. Her lifelong virginity is possible; but it never has been, and never can be proved. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/1-25.html
- **Gill:** lifelong virginity seems to be no necessary article of faith. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/1-25.html
- **Matthew Henry:** it cannot be proved from Scripture. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/1-25.html
- **Barnes:** the wording implies she lived as Joseph's wife after the birth. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/1-25.html
- **Jamieson-Fausset-Brown:** "till" does not necessarily mean things changed afterwards. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/1-25.htm
- **Chuck Smith** (Calvary Chapel) calls perpetual virginity a dogma without a scriptural basis. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/1-25.html
- **Anabaptist martyrs** told their interrogators that Scripture says nothing about it. https://ccel.org/ccel/vanbraght/mirror/mirror.iv.v.html?queryID=68239088&resultID=182699
- **GotQuestions and bible.org** both reject it. https://www.gotquestions.org/perpetual-virginity-Mary.html ; https://bible.org/book/export/html/23022

**v. 16 / vv. 12–16: How do the two genealogies fit together?** This is a split among evangelical teachers rather than between denominations.
- Guzik holds that Matthew gives Joseph's line and Luke gives Mary's.
- He also quotes Carson, who says the theory comes from the need to harmonise and that both Gospels seem to give Joseph's line.

https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-1/

## Other views

- **Catholic (v. 25):** heos ("until") need not imply a change afterwards. Catholic writers point to 2 Samuel 6:23 and quote Chrysostom that Matthew meant only that Mary was untouched before the birth. https://www.catholic.com/audio/cot/rebutted-top-objections-to-marys-perpetual-virginity
- **Catholic, on Jesus' "brothers":** they are understood as cousins. Catholic writers also cite the Protoevangelium of James (around AD 125), which says Joseph was a widower chosen to protect a consecrated virgin. https://www.catholic.com/tract/brethren-of-the-lord%C2%A0-%3E
- **Catholic (v. 23):** "almah" carried the sense of both youth and virginity. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/print-edition/virgin-birth
- **Theories that Matthew 1–2 is "midrash":** these say the chapters are imaginative stories rather than history. Guzik rejects this and quotes Carson that Matthew 1–2 has no running Old Testament text, as midrash would. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-1/
- **Not found:** modern scholarship from bibleodyssey/netbible, any Orthodox reading, and any prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on this chapter.
